Ascents to the divine realm were also a theme in Greco-Roman literature (e.g. Cicero's Dream of Scipio), but John's model is plainly prophetic and apocalyptic.

John is granted a heavenly vantage point from which to see earthly events in God's perspective. The trumpet-like voice is that of Revelation 1:10. Most interpreters treat the ascent as visionary ('in the Spirit'), not as a bodily removal.

Dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) take 'after these things' as marking the transition from the church age (chapters 2-3, 'the things that are', Revelation 1:19) to the future tribulation; many see John's summons as a picture or type of the pretribulation rapture, noting the church is not named on earth again until chapter 19. Others in the same camp treat it only as an illustration, not a proof text.

Preterists such as Gentry and Chilton read 'what must happen after these things' as events soon to come (Revelation 1:1, 3), chiefly the judgment of first-century Jerusalem and the vindication of the church; the ascent shows the heavenly court convening to pass that sentence.

Idealists and many eclectic scholars (Beale, Hendriksen) note the Daniel 2 allusion and argue that the 'latter days' have already begun with Christ's resurrection, so the visions that follow span the whole period between the first and second comings; John's ascent is a prophetic commissioning like Isaiah's or Ezekiel's.
Historicists (Elliott, Barnes) read the phrase as the opening of a prophetic panorama of history from John's day forward, beginning with the Roman empire, which the seals then trace in order.
At once I was in the Spirit

Ezekiel is repeatedly lifted by 'the Spirit' and carried in visions (Ezekiel 2:2, 3:12-14, 8:3, 11:1, 37:1). The phrase marks prophetic ecstasy rather than ordinary sight, as in Revelation 1:10, 17:3 and 21:10.
The four 'in the Spirit' notices (1:10, 4:2, 17:3, 21:10) are widely seen as structural markers, each opening a major visionary block. The phrase claims prophetic authority on the model of Ezekiel.
A throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it

Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven (1 Kings 22:19); Isaiah sees him 'high and lifted up' in the temple (Isaiah 6:1); Ezekiel sees a sapphire throne above the cherubim (Ezekiel 1:26-28); Daniel sees thrones set and the Ancient of Days seated (Daniel 7:9). 1 Enoch 14:18-20 describes a lofty crystal throne with streams of fire. Later rabbinic and Hekhalot mysticism meditated on this chariot-throne (merkavah), though those texts are later than Revelation. John reverently avoids describing God's form, naming him only 'the One seated on the throne'.
The emperor's throne (and the empty throne or curule chair displayed in imperial cult settings) symbolized Roman sovereignty; provincial assemblies and imperial temples in Asia displayed it publicly.

The throne is the controlling image of Revelation (the word occurs over forty times). It asserts that God, not Rome or Satan, rules history. Chapters 4-5 deliberately place all that follows under the throne's authority.
Looked like jasper and carnelian

Precious stones describe divine glory in Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:26. Jasper and carnelian (sardius) are among the twelve stones of the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-20) and of the Eden list in Ezekiel 28:13. Jasper reappears as the radiance of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:11, 18-19).

Ancient jasper ranged from green to translucent; carnelian was red-orange and was a common engraved gem in signet rings across the Roman world. Ancient stone names do not map neatly onto modern mineralogy, so the exact colours are uncertain.

God is described only by brilliance and colour, not form, guarding his transcendence. Many interpreters see a hint of holiness or glory (jasper) and judgment or redemption (red carnelian), but such colour-symbolism is speculative. The link to the high priest's stones and to the New Jerusalem ties God's throne to his dwelling with his people.
A rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne

Ezekiel describes the radiance around the throne as 'like the bow in the cloud on a day of rain' (Ezekiel 1:28). The bow recalls God's covenant with Noah and all creation never again to destroy the earth by flood (Genesis 9:12-17).
The Greek iris can mean a rainbow or a halo of light; an emerald-green halo was an unusual image and may reflect the emerald's prized brilliance in Roman jewellery.

The rainbow signals that the judgments about to fall come from a covenant-keeping God whose purpose is to preserve and renew creation, not merely to destroy it. It qualifies the lightning and thunder that follow with mercy.
Twenty-four elders on twenty-four thrones

David divided the priests into twenty-four courses (1 Chronicles 24:7-19) and the temple singers into twenty-four divisions who prophesied with lyres (1 Chronicles 25:9-31). Elders of Israel ascended Sinai and saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9-11), and Isaiah 24:23 pictures the LORD reigning gloriously 'before his elders'. Daniel 7:9 speaks of 'thrones' (plural) set in heaven. Twelve tribes plus twelve apostles is a pairing Revelation itself makes in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12-14).
Roman emperors ruled with a council (consilium) of advisers, and vassal kings sat in honour near the emperor; John's picture of a heavenly council would have been readily understood.
The elders share in God's rule and lead heaven's worship, offering prayers (5:8) and interpreting visions (5:5, 7:13). Their identity is one of the book's classic disputes.

Dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) usually identify them as the raptured, glorified church (perhaps with Old Testament saints), crowned and robed in white as promised to overcomers (Revelation 2:10, 3:5, 3:21), already in heaven before the tribulation judgments begin.

Many idealists and amillennial commentators (Hendriksen, Beale) see them as representing the whole people of God of both covenants, twelve patriarchs and twelve apostles, enthroned with Christ (Revelation 3:21) and leading heaven's liturgy, a symbol rather than a timetable marker.

A strong strand of critical and evangelical scholarship (Aune, Mounce, and others) takes them as an exalted order of angels forming God's heavenly council, noting they distinguish themselves from the saints in Revelation 5:8-10 (in the better-attested text) and serve as angelic interpreters in 7:13.

Chilton reads them as the heavenly counterpart of the twenty-four priestly courses: the church as a royal priesthood now officiating in the true temple, superseding the earthly priesthood of Jerusalem's temple.
Dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads
White linen was priestly dress (Leviticus 16:4) and the clothing of heavenly beings and the righteous in Daniel 7:9, 12:10 and 1 Enoch 62:15-16, where the elect are clothed in 'garments of glory'.

The stephanos was a victor's or festal wreath, often of gold for civic benefactors and priests of the imperial cult; Roman Asia's high priests wore golden crowns bearing images of the emperor. White garments were worn at festivals and by worshippers.

White signals purity and victory; golden wreaths signal shared royal honour. Both echo promises to the overcomers in Revelation 2-3 (2:10; 3:4-5, 11). Whether that echo identifies the elders with the redeemed is debated (see the twenty-four elders).
Flashes of lightning, rumblings and peals of thunder

Thunder, lightning and a trumpet blast accompany God's descent on Sinai (Exodus 19:16-19); lightning flashes from Ezekiel's living creatures (Ezekiel 1:13); storm imagery marks God's warrior presence in Psalm 18:12-14 and Psalm 77:18.
Greek and Roman religion associated thunderbolts with Zeus/Jupiter, a deity whose great altar stood at Pergamum; John assigns the storm to the God of Sinai.

These are theophanic signs of God's covenant presence and coming judgment. Bauckham shows that the formula recurs at the climax of each judgment series and grows each time (8:5, 11:19, 16:18-21), tying the seals, trumpets and bowls back to this throne.
Seven torches of fire, the seven Spirits of God

Zechariah sees a golden lampstand with seven lamps, explained as the Spirit's work and as 'the eyes of the LORD' ranging through the earth (Zechariah 4:2-10). Isaiah 11:2 (especially in the Greek and later Jewish reading) lists a sevenfold endowment of the Spirit on the Davidic branch. Fire before the throne recalls Ezekiel 1:13 and Daniel 7:10. Tobit 12:15 and 1 Enoch 20 speak of seven archangels before God.
Torches (lampades) were carried in civic and religious processions, including imperial festivals.

Most interpreters identify the 'seven Spirits' as the Holy Spirit in his fullness (seven = completeness), already named alongside the Father and Jesus in Revelation 1:4-5. A minority, citing Tobit and 1 Enoch, take them as seven chief angels. Placed before the throne in the temple-like setting, they also recall the seven-branched menorah.
Something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal

Above the cherubim Ezekiel sees an expanse 'like awesome crystal' (Ezekiel 1:22); the elders at Sinai saw beneath God's feet a pavement of sapphire, clear as the sky (Exodus 24:10). Genesis 1:6-7 places waters above the firmament. Solomon's temple had a huge bronze basin called 'the Sea' (1 Kings 7:23-26). In 1 Enoch 14:9-10 the heavenly house has a crystal floor. The sea is also the Old Testament symbol of chaos subdued by God (Psalm 74:13; Psalm 93:3-4; Daniel 7:2-3).
Glass was costly and rarely perfectly clear in antiquity; a vast transparent 'sea' would evoke unimaginable splendour. Many cities in Asia had glass-making industries.

The image conveys the transcendence and calm majesty of God's presence, and probably the heavenly counterpart of the temple's Sea. Many add that the chaotic sea, from which the beast later rises (13:1), is here calm before God; in 15:2 it is mixed with fire and the victors stand beside it like Israel beside the Red Sea, and in 21:1 the sea is no more.
Four living creatures: like a lion, a calf, a man and a flying eagle

Ezekiel's 'living creatures' (later identified as cherubim, Ezekiel 10:14-15, 20) each have four faces: man, lion, ox and eagle (Ezekiel 1:5-10). Cherubim guarded Eden and overshadowed the ark (Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18-22). Later rabbinic tradition (e.g. Exodus Rabbah 23:13) explains the faces as the kings of creation: the lion of wild beasts, the ox of cattle, the eagle of birds, and man over all; a later Targum tradition links them to the four standards of Israel's camp (Numbers 2), though both are later than Revelation.

Some scholars note that the lion, bull, man (Aquarius) and eagle (often associated with Scorpio) correspond to the four 'fixed' zodiac signs marking the cardinal points of the sky, suggesting the creatures stand at the four corners of the heavens; this astral background is debated.

Unlike Ezekiel's creatures, each of John's has a single face, and they combine features of cherubim and seraphim. They are commonly taken as the highest order of angels representing the whole of animate creation in ceaseless worship of the Creator. From Irenaeus onward (Against Heresies 3.11.8) Christian tradition also linked them with the four Gospels, a later devotional application rather than John's intent.
Covered with eyes in front and back, all around and within

In Ezekiel the rims of the wheels, and later the cherubim themselves, are 'full of eyes all around' (Ezekiel 1:18; 10:12). The seven eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10; 2 Chronicles 16:9).
The eyes express ceaseless vigilance and comprehensive knowledge: nothing in creation escapes the notice of God's throne. They prepare for the seven eyes of the Lamb (5:6).
Six wings; 'Holy, Holy, Holy' day and night

The six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6:2-3 cry the threefold holy (the Trisagion). 1 Enoch 39:12-13 has the watchers bless 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord of spirits' unceasingly, and 2 Enoch 21:1 has similar ceaseless praise. The Trisagion became the Kedushah of synagogue liturgy; how early that liturgical form was fixed is debated. Unceasing worship echoes the Levites who served 'day and night' (1 Chronicles 9:33).

Asia had professional choirs of 'hymn-singers' (hymnodoi) devoted to the divine Augustus and Roma, attested at Pergamum, who sang the emperor's praises at festivals. John's ceaseless heavenly choir offers a rival liturgy.
Holiness, God's utter otherness and moral purity, is the first note of heaven's worship and the ground of the judgments that follow. The repetition is a Hebrew superlative.
Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come

'Almighty' (pantokratōr) is the Greek Old Testament rendering of 'LORD of hosts' (YHWH Sabaoth), e.g. Amos 4:13 and Hosea 12:5. 'Who was and is and is to come' expands the divine name of Exodus 3:14 ('I AM WHO I AM'); later targumic tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Deuteronomy 32:39) paraphrases the name similarly as he who is, was and will be.

A Greek hymn recorded by Pausanias (10.12.10) praised 'Zeus who was, Zeus who is, Zeus who will be', and emperors carried titles of supreme power (autokratōr, imperator). John claims such titles for Israel's God alone.

God is eternal and sovereign over all times, and 'is to come' looks to his coming in judgment and salvation. Notably, in 11:17 and 16:5 the phrase 'is to come' drops out, because by then he has come to reign.
The elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne

Prostration (proskynēsis) before God is the posture of Old Testament worship (Psalm 95:6; 2 Chronicles 7:3). Kings of the earth bowing before Israel's God is a prophetic hope (Psalm 72:11; Isaiah 49:7).

Client kings showed submission by laying their crowns before the emperor; Tacitus (Annals 15.29) describes the Parthian prince Tiridates placing his diadem at the foot of Nero's statue, and he later received it back from Nero in Rome. Golden crowns were also presented to emperors by provincial cities.

The elders acknowledge that any authority or honour they possess derives from God and is returned to him. The scene subverts imperial ceremony: the true Sovereign, not Caesar, receives the crowns of the world's rulers.
'Worthy are You, our Lord and God ... for You created all things'
Praise of God as Creator is the basis of his claim on all things (Nehemiah 9:6; Psalm 33:6-9; Isaiah 40:26-28; 42:5). Creation and kingship are joined in the enthronement psalms (Psalm 93; 96:5, 10).

'Worthy!' (axios) was a public acclamation used when emperors entered cities or received honours. Suetonius (Domitian 13) says Domitian had himself styled 'our Lord and God' (dominus et deus noster) in official letters. On the late date this is a direct counter-claim; on an early date it still answers the general deification of emperors.

God's worthiness rests on his act of creation: he alone gives existence, so he alone deserves worship. The hymn's language transfers to God what the imperial cult claimed for Caesar, and it prepares for the parallel hymn to the Lamb in chapter 5 based on redemption.

Partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton) read chapters 4-5 as the heavenly court convening to judge apostate Israel in the generation of the apostles. Chilton stresses the covenant-lawsuit structure and the temple imagery: the true sanctuary is in heaven, served by a heavenly priesthood, as the earthly temple nears its destruction. God's sovereignty here assures persecuted first-century believers that their vindication is near (Revelation 1:1, 3).

Historicists (Elliott, Barnes) treat chapter 4 as the prophetic stage set before the panorama of church and world history from the first century onward. The throne vision establishes that the long succession of events in the seals (the decline of pagan Rome) and the trumpets (the barbarian and Islamic invasions) is governed by God.

Dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) see 4:1 as the turning point from the church age to the future seventieth week of Daniel. The church, represented by the crowned and white-robed elders, is already in heaven, consistent with a pretribulation rapture, and chapters 4-5 depict the heavenly preparation for the coming tribulation judgments. Historic premillennial futurists (Ladd) share the future orientation of the judgments but do not see a rapture in 4:1.

Idealists (Hendriksen, Poythress) see the throne room as the permanent reality behind all of history: in every age the church must see that God reigns before it can face persecution. The chapter is less a moment in a sequence than the vantage point for interpreting all that follows.

Eclectic scholars (Beale, Osborne, Mounce) emphasize that the chapter is modeled on Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 1, presenting God's sovereignty over history and creation, with immediate relevance to Roman Asia and the imperial cult, and a trajectory toward the consummation. Beale reads Revelation 4-5 as a vision of Christ's inaugurated rule since his resurrection, expressed in the church-age judgments of the seals.
Why do you think John begins the visions of judgment with a scene of worship rather than with the judgments themselves?
Which details of chapter 4 come from Ezekiel 1, Isaiah 6 and Exodus 19? What does combining them communicate?
Who are the twenty-four elders? Weigh the case for the raptured church, the whole people of God and an angelic council.
How might believers in a city with an imperial temple have heard the acclamation 'our Lord and God'?
Does 'what must happen after these things' (Revelation 4:1) point to the near future, the whole church age or the end times? What in the text decides it?
The Scroll and the Lamb

In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one in all creation is found worthy to open it, so John weeps. An elder announces the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, as the one who has conquered, but John turns and sees a Lamb standing as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes. The Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven erupts in a new song: he is worthy because by his blood he has ransomed a people from every nation and made them a kingdom and priests. The worship widens to myriads of angels and then to every creature, and God and the Lamb are praised together.
The sealed scroll and the search for one worthy
The Lion who is a Lamb takes the scroll
The new song of the creatures and elders
Myriads of angels: 'Worthy is the Lamb'
All creation praises God and the Lamb

Chapter 5 completes the throne vision and turns it toward action. Its backbone, many scholars argue, is Daniel 7: a figure approaches the enthroned Ancient of Days amid myriads of attendants, receives dominion over all peoples, nations and languages, and books are opened. Ezekiel 2:9-3:3 supplies the scroll written front and back, and Daniel 12:4, 9 and Isaiah 29:11 supply the motif of a sealed book whose contents await God's appointed time. Jewish messianic hope is invoked by name (Lion of Judah from Genesis 49:9-10; Root of David from Isaiah 11:1, 10), and 4 Ezra 11-12 pictures the Messiah as a lion who rebukes and destroys an eagle that stands for Rome. Against that expectation John sees a slaughtered Lamb, drawing on Passover (Exodus 12), the daily temple offerings, and the servant led like a lamb to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7).

Culturally, the scroll would evoke legal documents: Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses, and contracts and deeds were often 'double documents' with a sealed inner text and an open summary (compare Jeremiah 32:10-14 and deeds found in the Judaean desert). The worship borrows from both the temple (harps, golden bowls of incense, priests) and the imperial court, whose acclamations and hymns hailed the emperor as worthy of power, wealth and glory. John's key move is that the Lamb shares the throne and receives the same worship as God (5:13), a striking expression of early Jewish-Christian devotion to Jesus within Jewish monotheism (Bauckham).
A scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne, written on both sides

Ezekiel is handed a scroll written 'on the front and back' with lament, mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9-10). Daniel is told to seal up the book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9), and books are opened at the judgment (Daniel 7:10). Jeremiah's purchase deed was sealed and an open copy kept (Jeremiah 32:10-14). 1 Enoch 81 and 93 speak of heavenly tablets recording the destiny of humankind.

A scroll written on both sides (an opisthograph) was unusual but known. Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses (Gaius, Institutes 2.119) and could be opened only on the testator's death; deeds and contracts, as in the Babatha archive from the Judaean desert, were often doubled with a sealed inner text.

The scroll contains God's sovereign plan for judging evil and establishing his kingdom; its unfolding begins with the seals. 'Both sides' stresses its fullness. Exactly what kind of document it is, and what it contains, is disputed.

Walvoord and many dispensationalists see it as the title deed of the earth (on the model of the kinsman-redeemer and Jeremiah 32): Christ, as redeemer, takes legal possession of the world, and the seals, trumpets and bowls of the future tribulation are the process of reclaiming it.

Chilton (following Ford and others) suggests it is the covenant document, even a bill of divorce, against unfaithful Israel, written like the tablets of the covenant on both sides (Exodus 32:15), whose curses fall on Jerusalem in AD 70 as the seals are broken.

Hendriksen and Beale take it as God's decree for history and redemption (Beale: the plan of judgment and redemption first foretold in Daniel), which Christ began to execute at his resurrection and ascension and which governs the whole church age.
Historicists (Elliott, Barnes) see it as the scroll of future history, whose seals and trumpets unveil successive eras of the Roman empire and the church from John's day onward.

Others, citing Roman testamentary practice, read it as a last will or testament whose inheritance (the kingdom) is released through the death of the testator, the slain Lamb; Bauckham and others hold that its main content is revealed only from chapter 10 onward, when the scroll lies open.
Sealed with seven seals

Sealing a prophetic book reserves its fulfilment for God's time (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9; Isaiah 8:16; 29:11). Seven is the covenant number of completeness, and Leviticus 26 threatens sevenfold covenant chastisements (Leviticus 26:18, 21, 24, 28).
Wax or clay seals impressed with a signet authenticated and secured documents; breaking them was reserved for an authorized person. Seven witness seals on Roman wills is a commonly cited parallel.

The scroll is completely sealed: its contents are inaccessible and inoperative until the authorized one opens it. In Revelation the seals are broken one by one in chapter 6, suggesting that the opening of the plan sets judgment in motion.
'Who is worthy to break the seals?' No one in heaven, on earth or under the earth

Heaven, earth and the underworld form the three-tiered Old Testament picture of the cosmos (Exodus 20:4; Psalm 115:16-17). The 'mighty angel' recalls the angelic heralds of Daniel 4:13-14 and the angel Gabriel ('might of God'). Weeping over a hidden revelation resembles the seer's distress in 4 Ezra 5:13 and 2 Baruch 9-10.
Heralds made public proclamations at games and assemblies, calling for a qualified claimant to step forward.

The unanswered challenge underlines that no created being, not even angels, can carry out God's purposes of judgment and redemption. John's tears express the anguish of a world without that resolution, and set up the revelation of the Lamb.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah

Jacob blesses Judah as a lion's cub from whom the scepter will not depart (Genesis 49:9-10), a text read messianically in the Targums and at Qumran (4Q252). In 4 Ezra 11:36-12:34 the Messiah appears as a lion who indicts and destroys the eagle that represents Rome. 1 Maccabees 3:4 likens Judas Maccabeus to a lion in battle.
The lion was a widespread image of royal power in the Near East and Rome; the eagle, the lion's foe in 4 Ezra, was Rome's legionary standard.

The title evokes Jewish expectation of a conquering Davidic king from Judah. The elder announces that this Messiah 'has triumphed' (enikēsen, the same verb as the promises to overcomers), and the ground of that victory is revealed in the next verse.
The Root of David has triumphed

Isaiah foretells a shoot from the stump of Jesse and a 'root of Jesse' who stands as a banner for the nations (Isaiah 11:1, 10); Jeremiah speaks of a righteous Branch for David (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15). Qumran texts expect a 'Branch of David' who will arise at the end (4Q161 on Isaiah 11; 4Q174; 4Q285), and Sirach 47:22 speaks of a root from David's line.

Jesus is the promised Davidic Messiah who fulfils the royal covenant (2 Samuel 7). In Revelation 22:16 he is both root and offspring of David, the source as well as the descendant of David's line. His triumph is a completed act, pointing to the cross and resurrection.
A Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne

The Passover lamb's blood delivered Israel from judgment and slavery (Exodus 12); lambs were offered morning and evening in the daily tamid sacrifice (Exodus 29:38-42); the suffering servant was led 'like a lamb to the slaughter' (Isaiah 53:7). In the Animal Apocalypse of 1 Enoch 89-90, God's people are sheep and a horned lamb or ram leads them in victorious battle (1 Enoch 90:9-13). Testament of Joseph 19:8 has a conquering lamb, though that passage may contain Christian additions.
Sacrificial lambs were a familiar sight in temples throughout the Greco-Roman world. 'Slain' (esphagmenon) is the language of sacrificial slaughter and of execution.

This is the theological centre of the book. John hears of a Lion but sees a Lamb: the Messiah conquers through sacrificial death, and the marks of slaughter remain on the risen ('standing') Christ. Bauckham calls it a rebirth of images, redefining messianic victory. The Lamb stands at the centre of the throne, sharing God's rule; 'Lamb' becomes Christ's dominant title in Revelation (some 28 times).
Seven horns and seven eyes, the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth

Horns signify power and kingship (Deuteronomy 33:17; 1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 89:17; Daniel 7:7-8, 24; 8:3-8); in 1 Enoch 90:9 a great horn sprouts on a lamb who leads the flock. Zechariah's seven eyes are 'the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth' (Zechariah 4:10; compare 3:9).

The Lamb has complete power (seven horns) and complete knowledge and presence through the Spirit (seven eyes). The Spirits that stood before the throne in 4:5 are now 'sent out into all the earth' by the Lamb, suggesting the Spirit's mission following Christ's exaltation (compare John 15:26; Acts 2:33).
He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne

In Daniel 7:13-14 one like a son of man comes before the Ancient of Days and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom so that all peoples, nations and languages serve him. Psalm 110:1 seats the Messiah at God's right hand.
Investiture ceremonies, in which authority passed to a successor or appointee, were familiar from Roman and Hellenistic court life.
The Lamb's taking of the scroll is the decisive act of investiture: he receives authority to carry out God's plan for history. Many link it to Christ's ascension and enthronement.

Idealists and many amillennial interpreters (Hendriksen, Beale) identify the scene with Christ's ascension and enthronement (Acts 2:33-36; Ephesians 1:20-22; Hebrews 1:3): from that moment he governs history, so the seals describe the whole church age.
Partial preterists likewise see the ascension, Christ receiving the kingdom of Daniel 7:13-14, after which he executes covenant judgment on Jerusalem within that generation.

Dispensational futurists usually see a heavenly scene still future, after the rapture, when Christ initiates the tribulation judgments that lead to his visible reign; some acknowledge that his worthiness rests on the past cross while the act of opening is future.
Historicists generally place the investiture at Christ's exaltation and read the following seals as beginning in the late first or second century.
Each one had a harp
The kinnor (Greek kithara) accompanied psalm singing (Psalm 33:2; 98:5; 147:7). The Levitical singers in their twenty-four divisions 'prophesied with lyres' (1 Chronicles 25:1-6).
The kithara was the instrument of Apollo and of professional singers; Nero famously performed as a citharode and competed in Greek musical contests.
The harps mark the elders' worship as temple song in the tradition of the Levitical choirs, celebrating a new act of salvation. The harp reappears with the redeemed in 14:2 and 15:2.
Golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints

David prays that his prayer be counted as incense (Psalm 141:2). The golden altar of incense stood before the veil and was tended morning and evening (Exodus 30:1-8); worshippers prayed outside at the hour of incense (Luke 1:9-10). Angels present prayers to God in Tobit 12:12-15, and in 3 Baruch 11-14 the archangel Michael carries a great bowl receiving the prayers and virtues of the righteous.
Offering a pinch of incense before the emperor's image was a standard test of loyalty, as Pliny the Younger's letter to Trajan (Letters 10.96) shows for Christians in Bithynia c. 112.

The prayers of persecuted believers rise before God as fragrant offering. They are not forgotten: in 8:3-5 incense and prayers are offered on the golden altar and then fire is hurled to the earth, linking the saints' prayers to God's acts of judgment and vindication.
They sang a new song

A 'new song' greets a fresh act of divine victory or deliverance in the Psalms and Isaiah (Psalm 33:3; 40:3; 96:1; 98:1; 144:9; 149:1; Isaiah 42:10). Israel's archetypal song of redemption is the Song of the Sea after the Exodus (Exodus 15).
